newsitem.title: UK: Legal challenge to UK windfall tax seen tough.
newsitem.headline: Legal challenge to UK windfall tax seen tough.

text.p: British companies attempting to launch a legal challenge against the Labour government's proposed windfall tax on "excess profits" could find it an uphill task, industry and legal sources said on Friday.
"It is difficult to see how this gets off the ground, it would be hard work but it is not impossible," said one source with a legal firm.

On Thursday, British Telecommunications (BT) chairman Sir Iain Vallance said the group owed it to its investors to challenge such a tax "if we are stung in a big way and if it can be challenged legally."
British Airports Authority (BAA) joined the fray, saying it was taking legal advice and accusing Labour of "verging on irresponsibility" by not detailing who would be hit.

The new Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, has made a one-off windfall tax on utilities to finance programmes to get 250,000 young people back to work a mainstay of its policy.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown is expected to announce details of the tax in his first budget, likely in June or July.

Labour's target of "excess profits" of privatised utilities for the tax could cast a net wide enough to include BT, the former British Gas utility Centrica and even Railtrack and BAA, as well as water and electricity companies.

Labour maintains that there are no legal, financial nor technical obstacles to the levy, while Brown has said the tax should "comfortably" cover the three billion pounds($4.9 billion) cost of the unemployment plans.
BT has maintained that it should not be subject to the tax because it is not a monopoly nor a utility and has not made excess profits.
But on Sunday, the Observer newspaper quoted paymaster general Geoffrey Robinson saying it was "hard to see how (BT) could be left out."

BT's Vallance said it "could be that the way in which they have to structure the bill is such that we would need to be considered, but there is a long, long step from being considered to being taxed."

Some analysts suggest that the government will construct a framework covering a broad base of companies to avoid challenges of discrimination, but will then use assessment formulae to target a narrower range of firms.
If BT were to mount a legal challenge, its most likely gambit would be under European law, analysts said, as Labour's strong mandate makes a case under domestic law hard to sustain.
The company might claim that the windfall tax unfairly penalised it and was therefore against European Community competition law, according to Ian Gibson, a tax partner at Frere Cholmeley Bischoff.
"The windfall tax, it could be argued, would have the effect of a negative subsidy, that it would be disadvantaging," he said.

In effect, BT might hope to claim that the tax unfairly penalised it against competitors, the reverse of most cases which claim state subsidies give an advantage in areas such as airlines and car manufacture.
"It would involve an enlargement of theory and there is no precedent for this," Gibson said.
If BT were to challenge in European courts, it could also face some political reservations, analysts said.
The new Labour government is enjoying a honeymoon period of improved relations with its European partners, appearing to have a much more positive stance than the former Conservative government.
European partners might be unwilling to make a judgement against the fledgling government on such an important part of its economic and social policy, observers said.
And the EU has scant tradition of interfering in the domestic tax policies of its member states, they add.
Water and electricity companies, meanwhile, appear largely resigned to paying a windfall tax, which could aim to bring in around five billion pounds to treasury coffers.

These utilities, privatised at the beginning of the decade under the previous Conservative government, have been fiercely criticised by Labour for hefty shareholder payouts and profits, as well as chunky executive pay packets.
"There is going to be a windfall tax and we are going to have to pay it," said a spokeswoman for Hyder, the Wales-based water and electricity group.
"Our prime concern is to ensure that (the tax) is a one-off, at a reasonable level and that it is fair and equitable," said a spokesman for United Utilities.
($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
